notes.summary: The amphibians still alive today, which fall into three orders: frogs and toads, salamanders and newts, and the burrowing caecilians.

words.note: A tailless amphibian built for jumping; frogs and toads together make up the order Anura.
A salamander of the newt subfamily, which lives on land as an adult but returns to water to breed.
The tailed amphibians, order Caudata, which keep their tails into adulthood where a frog loses its.
A frog, informally — the word picks out the drier, wartier, shorter-legged ones rather than a group of its own.

notes.summary: Hounds hunt by scent or by sight, which is what separates them from the gundogs and the terriers.

words.note: The basset hound: short legs and long ears, bred in France to trail game slowly enough to follow on foot.
A small scent hound bred in England for hunting hare.
The scent hound with the keenest nose of any breed, able to follow a trail hours or days old.
A sighthound, which runs its quarry down by sight and speed rather than by scent; the fastest dog there is.

notes.summary: The four years of an American undergraduate degree, each with a name of its own.

words.note: First year.
Third year.
Fourth year, and the last one.
Second year; traditionally read as the Greek for 'wise' and 'foolish' at once.

notes.summary: Four adjectives for the most important one of a set — each of which also has a second life as a noun.

words.note: Foremost, as in chief executive; as a noun, the head of a group.
The principal one, as in the main road.
Greater or more important, as in a major road; also an army rank.
First in importance or in quality, as in prime minister.

notes.summary: Four kinds of clip, each named either for what it grips or for what it grips like.

words.note: An alligator clip has serrated jaws that meet like a set of teeth; used to make a temporary electrical connection.
A binder clip squeezes a stack of paper between two folding steel handles.
A bulldog clip is the sprung metal paper clamp, named for the grip.
The paper clip: a single loop of bent wire.

notes.summary: The brass section — instruments sounded by buzzing the lips into a mouthpiece.

words.note: The French horn: a coiled brass instrument, played with one hand inside the bell.
The brass instrument that changes pitch on a sliding tube rather than with valves.
The highest of the standard brass, with three valves.
The lowest brass instrument, and the foundation the section is built on.

notes.summary: Eponyms: everyday words that started out as somebody's name.

words.note: Charles Boycott, the Irish land agent whose tenants refused to deal with him in 1880.
The 7th Earl of Cardigan, a British commander in the Crimean War, whose officers wore knitted woollen waistcoats.
Rudolf Diesel, the German engineer who patented the compression-ignition engine.
Adolphe Sax, the Belgian instrument maker who invented it in the 1840s.

notes.summary: To forbid with authority behind it, rather than merely to disapprove.

words.note: To forbid outright.
To make something illegal; of a person, once, to put them outside the protection of the law altogether.
To forbid by law or by rule.
To block a decision that has already been taken; Latin for 'I forbid', and the word a Roman tribune used to do it.

notes.summary: The shape of the leg, which is how denim is sold.

words.note: Narrow to the knee, then widening just enough to sit over a boot.
Widening from the knee down, and more sharply than a bootcut does.
Close-fitting the whole length of the leg.
The same width from the knee to the ankle.

notes.summary: Tops cut without sleeves, each named for the way it stays up.

words.note: Tied behind the neck, leaving the shoulders and back bare; a halter is also a rope headcollar for a horse.
The tank top, named after the tank suit — the one-piece costume worn in a swimming tank.
A strapless band of stretch fabric, held up by nothing but its own tension.
In British use a sleeveless undershirt; in American use, a waistcoat.

notes.summary: Four of the English weekday names come from Norse gods; the other three come from the sun, the moon and Saturn.

words.note: Tiw's day — Tiw, or Tyr, the god of single combat.
Woden's day — Woden, or Odin, the chief of the gods.
Thor's day: thunder, and the hammer.
Frigg's day — Frigg, Odin's wife.

notes.summary: Four compounds ending in DRIVER, and only one of them is a person driving anything.

words.note: A screwdriver turns screws.
A pile driver hammers piles into the ground; also, a wrestling move.
A Sunday driver is a slow and hesitant one, out for the drive rather than to arrive.
A backseat driver tells the actual driver what to do from behind them.

notes.summary: The woodwinds that sound a reed, which is the distinction that leaves the flute out.

words.note: Single reed, cylindrical bore.
Double reed, and the instrument the rest of the orchestra tunes to.
Double reed, and the bass of the woodwind section.
Single reed, and made of brass — but a woodwind, because the reed is what decides it.

notes.summary: Named glasses, each shaped for what goes in it.

words.note: A flat-bottomed glass with no stem and no handle.
A bowl on a stem, on a foot.
A short-stemmed balloon glass for brandy, narrowing at the top to hold the aroma in.
Tall and narrow, for sparkling wine — the shape is what keeps the bubbles.

notes.summary: The bodywork: the parts of a car you can put a hand on without opening anything.

words.note: The bar at each end that takes a low-speed impact.
The panel over a wheel arch; the American term for what British English calls a wing.
The slotted opening at the front that lets air through to the radiator.
The panel over the engine; the American term for a bonnet.
